insight.title: Access barriers concentrate with building burden
insight.claim: Among the 200 buildings with the most open violations, the share of open violations stuck in “FIRST NO ACCESS TO RE-INSPECT” is about double the citywide rate — suggesting chronic open inventories are not only about issuance volume, but also about failed re-inspection access.
insight.why_non_obvious: Borough-level concentration is surprisingly similar (top 10% of buildings hold ~49–53% of open violations in every borough). The sharper difference shows up in status composition: high-burden buildings are enriched for no-access reinspection states, while informational Class I violations almost disappear from their open inventory.

finding.title: Top-burden buildings look like multi-dwelling / multi-story stock
finding.scope: Top 200 buildings by distinct open violationid
finding.method_note: Open HPD Violations do not include official unit counts or building class. We proxy structure from distinct non-blank apartment and story values among each building’s currently open violations. This can understate true size (violations may touch only some units) and cannot prove a building is 1–2 family.
finding.summary: Among the top 200 buildings, 188 (94.0%) show a clear multi-dwelling complex signal (many distinct apartments and/or high floors with opens). Only 0 show a limited apartment/story signal — and even those are not proof of single-family stock. Minimum distinct apartments with opens in this top-200 set: 3.

finding.title: Class B is the lingering open backlog — Class C turns over faster
finding.claim: Open Class B violations are substantially older than open Class C: 50% of citywide open Class B was inspected before 2020, versus 32% of Class C (median inspection years 2019 vs 2023). In the top 200 buildings, open inventory is newer overall — but Class B still ages out more slowly than Class C (17% vs 11% pre-2020). The stuck open book is Class B persistence, not Class C “hazard permanence.”
finding.why_non_obvious: It is natural to assume the most serious hazards (Class C) are what linger. The age profile of currently open violations shows the opposite: immediately hazardous opens recycle faster, while Class B accumulates as long-lived backlog — citywide and inside the highest-burden buildings.
finding.method_note: Age uses inspectiondate year for distinct open violationid rows. Years before 1980 are dropped as date-quality outliers. “Pre-2020” means inspection year ≤ 2019.

finding.title: Chronic buildings over-index on moisture/leak problems; their Class C opens are pest-heavy
finding.claim: Relative to the citywide open inventory, the top 200 buildings are enriched for Mold / moisture (1.7×), Paint / surfaces (non-lead) (1.51×), and Water leak / plumbing (1.5×). Separately, among Class C (immediately hazardous) opens in those buildings, Pests / infestation is the leading primary theme at 35.8% — not a uniform mix of hazards.
finding.why_non_obvious: High open counts could just be “more of the same” problem mix. Instead, chronic buildings skew toward moisture/leak/paint-type issues versus the city, while their most serious (Class C) open inventory is concentrated in pest cases — a specific remediation and access problem, not generic volume.
finding.method_note: Themes are keyword matches on novdescription. Citywide rates use SODA LIKE counts over distinct violationid (a violation can match multiple themes). Top-200 rates use the same keyword rules on deduped open rows pulled for those buildings. Primary theme = first matching rule in a fixed priority order.

finding.title: Chronic open inventories are multi-dwelling Class B moisture — not old Class C in small homes
finding.statement: Buildings with the most open violations are almost entirely multi-dwelling (188 of 200 in the top 200; 0 limited-unit / single-ish). In that tier, Class B mold/water is 11.4% of opens versus 7.5% citywide — a burden gradient that also appears in the next 200 (10.2%). Age×theme ties this to the Class B backlog channel: open Class B is much older than open Class C (50% vs 32% inspected before 2020). Class B mold/water sits in that Class B channel (36% pre-2020; median 2022) — older than Class C (32%, median 2023), though not older than other Class B themes (53%, median 2019). Limited-unit buildings show up mainly in lower-burden stock (34 of 200 in the lower-burden band) and do not drive the extreme open-violation tail.
finding.specificity: Three locks: (1) Structure — top 200 = 188 multi-dwelling / 12 small-multi / 0 limited-unit by apartment/story proxy. (2) Composition gradient — Class B∧mold|water share of opens: citywide 7.5% → lower-burden 7.6% → next 200 10.2% → top 200 11.4%. (3) Age×theme — pre-2020 shares: Class B other 53%, Class B mold/water 36%, all opens 40%, Class C 32%.
finding.non_obvious: Two common stories fail: that chronic opens are mostly lingering Class C hazards, and that “small homes with bad conditions” explain the worst open counts. The open tail is multi-dwelling; its distinctive overload is Class B moisture/mold volume; and the long-lived open book runs through Class B (with moisture as the enrichment in high-burden buildings), while Class C turns over younger.
arguments_for: Zero limited-unit / single-ish buildings in the top 200 open-violation tier (0 of 200); nearly all are multi-dwelling proxies.
Class B∧mold|water intensifies with burden: 7.5% of citywide opens vs 11.4% in the top 200 (and 10.2% in the next 200 — not only the extreme tip).
Age×theme: open Class B is the persistent channel vs Class C (50% vs 32% pre-2020). Class B mold/water is older than Class C (36% vs 32% pre-2020).
Mold/water NOV text is ~75% Class B citywide, so the moisture theme and the Class B backlog are the same enforcement channel.
arguments_against: Within Class B, non-moisture opens are even older than mold/water (53% vs 36% pre-2020) — so “persistence” is Class B broadly; moisture is the high-burden composition signature, not uniquely the oldest theme.
Apartment/story proxies are not official unit counts; limited-unit can be a large building with opens in few units.
Open-only data: age differences can reflect certification/closure pathways and inspection timing, not only physical duration of bad conditions.
Keyword matching on novdescription can miss or over-include some moisture-related wording.
HPD open violations underrepresent owner-occupied / non-regulated 1–2 family housing — the single-dwelling comparison is within the HPD open universe.
finding.method_note: Open HPD Violations only; distinct violationid. Moisture/mold = keyword match on novdescription (mold/mildew/leak/plumbing/water damage). Building structure proxy from distinct apartment + story labels among each building’s open violations: multi_dwelling (≥10 apts or ≥5 apts with floor≥4), small_multi (≥3 apts or multi-floor), limited_unit (few apt/floor labels — single-ish signal, not a deed/occupancy proof). Age uses inspectiondate year; years <1980 dropped.
finding.one_sentence: Prioritize Class B mold/water remediation in high-burden multi-dwelling buildings, where those opens are 11.4% of the inventory versus 7.5% citywide — while limited-unit / single-ish buildings are absent from the top-200 open-violation tier (0 of 200).

finding.title: Mold & moisture outrank pests in high-burden multi-dwellings
finding.statement: Across all currently open HPD violations citywide, pests appear in 14.6% of opens while mold & moisture (mold, leaks, plumbing, water damage) appear in 10.1%. In the multi-dwelling buildings among the top 200 by open-violation count (188 buildings, 102,474 opens), that ranking flips: mold & moisture are 16.1% of opens versus pests at 11.6%.
finding.one_sentence: In high-burden multi-dwelling buildings, mold & moisture (16.1% of open violations) are more common than pests (11.6%) — the reverse of the citywide pattern (pests 14.6% vs moisture 10.1%).
finding.why_it_matters: Pests are a familiar, high-volume citywide issue. In the buildings that carry the heaviest open-violation load — almost all multi-dwelling — mold and moisture problems take a larger share of the open inventory than pest problems do.
finding.method_note: Open HPD Violations only (csn4-vhvf); distinct violationid. Mold & moisture = NOV text match for mold/mildew/leak/plumbing/water damage. Pests = NOV text match for roach/mice/vermin/infestation/bedbug/rats. A violation can match both themes. Multi-dwelling = apartment/story proxy among each building’s open violations (≥10 distinct apartments, or ≥5 apartments with floor ≥4). Top 200 = buildings with the most open violations.
caveats: Keyword matching on violation descriptions can miss or over-include some wording.
Apartment/story proxies are not official unit counts.
Shares can overlap (one open violation may mention both moisture and pests).
